text: SSH is how you reach almost every Linux server you'll ever administer remotely — an encrypted connection for a shell, a file copy, or a tunnel. Password authentication works, but key-based authentication is both more secure and more convenient once it's set up, which is why Northbridge Retail requires it for every engineer touching a production server.

The first time you connect to a new host, SSH shows a fingerprint and asks you to confirm it before continuing. That's SSH recording the server's identity so it can warn you later if that identity ever changes unexpectedly, which could mean the server was rebuilt or something far less innocent.

A key pair has two halves: a private key that never leaves your machine, and a public key you hand to any server you want to access. When you connect, the server challenges your client to prove it holds the matching private key, and your key answers that challenge mathematically — a password is never involved at all.

ssh-keygen generates that key pair, creating a private file to keep secret and a public file that's safe to share. ssh-copy-id then does the sharing for you in one step, appending your public key to the authorized_keys file on the remote server so future connections need no password prompt at all.

scp copies files to or from a remote host using that exact same authentication. And since typing a full hostname and username gets old fast, ~/.ssh/config lets you define a short alias per host, so ssh web01 connects exactly as if you'd typed the whole thing.

Key-based SSH access is the foundation almost every other remote administration task in this course builds on. Up next, chapter six, lesson twenty-six: securing a Linux server, for locking down SSH itself and everything else exposed on this box.
